paragraphs: They claimed that the Torah was in the hands of the community as a single copy during the era of [Israelite] sovereignty, and that it expanded only afterwards. The people, on this view, learned the farāʾiḍ only by oral instruction (talqīn) from one another. The proponent argued from Scripture: Deut 31:9, "Moses wrote this Torah and delivered it to the priests the sons of Levi…," and Deut 31:26, "Take this book of the law and place it beside the ark…" — i.e., he transmitted to them a single copy and commanded them to set it beside the Ark as a witness. There was no other manuscript. He also argued from the king's law, Deut 17:18, "And he shall write for himself a copy of this Torah in a book" — for had the Torah been widely available, why would the king need to be commanded, on ascending the throne, to write a copy from the priests and Levites? He also argued from Deut 31:10–11, "at the end of every seventh year, in the year of release, at the feast of Sukkot, when all Israel comes to appear …" and v. 11, "read this Torah in their hearing." If Torah-copies were everywhere available and all could read them, why would Moses command a septennial reading?

He further argued from the book Hilkiah found in the house of the Lord (2 Kgs 22:8): "I have found the book of the law in the house of the Lord." Had the Torah been universal among the people, what would be remarkable about finding the book? So, on the Rabbanite position, the community in the era of sovereignty was not reading the Torah, and this was not obligatory upon them. What I myself think — Q here speaking in his own voice, breaking from the ḥikāya — is that this Rabbanite case is the foundation for the further Rabbanite claim that this Torah we currently have is not the Torah Moses brought — for the original was a single copy which either perished in the destruction of the Temple or was concealed with the Ark. (Josiah is said to have concealed the Ark when he knew the end was near and the enemy would burn the Temple.)[{2}] ---
